data.name: Bermuda
data.detailed_description:
A camp trip goes wrong for Edward and his friends as they are abducted into an alien submarine. They now await to hear if they will be allowed home, or be executed inside this ship. Edward wants to trust the aliens will make the right choice, but as the decision looms, doubt begins to whisper in his mind.

Bermuda is a visual novel mixed with open ended stealth puzzles. The game is fully voiced, featuring the talent of veteran actors such as Cristina Vee (Madoka Magica), Kira Buckland (Blue Exorcist) and Kyle Hebert (Dragonball). Xanthe Huynh and Skyler Davenport from Unhack also make a return, as well as voice actor Miguel Moran. For players who prefer to read the story like a traditional novel, each character's voice can be toggled individually.

Running at around an hour in length, Bermuda aims to be a succinct story that players can enjoy around their busy schedules. Each episode features bonus conversations, giving players a chance to know the cast better.

Illustrations: Alastair Sew Hoy
Music: Matt Hamm

A demo version of Bermuda is available! Please consider checking it out first to ensure the game runs well on your machine.

Thank you! I hope you will find the experience valuable.

reviews.review:
Bermuda takes a compact visual novel premise and gives it an unusual interactive twist, combining science-fiction storytelling with open-ended stealth puzzles. Developed and published by InvertMouse, it follows Edward and his friends after a camping trip goes disastrously wrong and they are abducted into an alien submarine. Instead of immediately searching for a heroic escape, the group finds itself waiting for a judgment that could either send them home or result in their execution. Edward initially wants to believe that their captors will make the right decision, but uncertainty gradually begins to undermine that confidence. The resulting story revolves around trust, deception, fear, and the psychological pressure of being powerless in an unfamiliar environment.

The alien submarine is an effective setting because it creates isolation without requiring an enormous world. The characters are confined to a place they do not understand and must deal with beings whose intentions remain uncertain. Much of the tension consequently comes from anticipation rather than constant action. Edward's growing doubts become an important part of the narrative, allowing the story to examine whether trusting an apparently rational authority is sensible when the consequences of that trust could be fatal. The premise is straightforward, but its mixture of alien captivity and interpersonal uncertainty gives the adventure a distinctive personality.

Gameplay separates itself from conventional visual novels through stealth puzzle sequences. Rather than simply reading conversations and advancing through illustrations, players encounter sections that require more direct interaction. These puzzles are relatively modest in complexity, but they fit the narrative because sneaking around an alien vessel naturally reinforces the vulnerability of the protagonists. The open-ended approach also gives these sequences some flexibility instead of reducing every challenge to a single rigid solution. Players looking for an elaborate stealth game should keep their expectations measured, however, because narrative remains the central attraction. The stealth mechanics are better understood as an interactive extension of the story than as the foundation of a deep mechanical system.

One of the stronger aspects of the presentation is the full English voice acting. The cast includes Cristina Vee, Kira Buckland, Kyle Hebert, Xanthe Huynh, Skyler Davenport, and Miguel Moran, giving the relatively small production a surprisingly substantial vocal component. Voice performances help establish personalities quickly, which is particularly valuable in such a short narrative. Players who prefer traditional visual-novel reading are not forced to use every performance either, as individual character voices can be toggled separately. This is a thoughtful feature that allows the presentation to accommodate both players who enjoy voiced dialogue and those who would rather control the pace of conversations themselves.

The visual and musical presentation complements the unusual premise without trying to overwhelm it. Illustrations by Alastair Sew Hoy give the characters an anime-influenced identity, while music by Matt Hamm supports the mixture of science fiction, mystery, and uneasiness. The presentation is naturally limited by the scale of the project, yet it generally serves the narrative well. The combination of illustrated characters, voice acting, music, and interactive puzzle sequences makes the experience feel more involved than a completely static visual novel, even though its production remains intentionally modest.

Its greatest strength and weakness is its brevity. The story is designed to last around an hour, making it possible to experience the complete narrative in a single sitting. This keeps the pacing focused and makes the game appealing to anyone who wants a self-contained story without a major time commitment. The downside is that the premise feels capable of supporting considerably more development. The alien society, relationships between the characters, and psychological implications of their predicament could all have benefited from additional exploration. Bonus conversations attached to the episodes provide extra opportunities to learn about the cast, but they cannot entirely compensate for the limited amount of time available for deeper characterization.

The concise structure nevertheless works for players who approach it as an interactive science-fiction short story rather than a sprawling adventure. There is little room for unnecessary padding, and the narrative reaches its central conflicts quickly. Its blend of visual-novel storytelling and stealth puzzles also prevents the experience from becoming entirely passive. Conversely, anyone expecting extensive exploration, complex stealth systems, lengthy character arcs, or a large number of gameplay scenarios may find the experience too slight. Its appeal lies more in its experimental combination of ideas than in mechanical or narrative scale.

Steam Deck compatibility deserves some caution. The game has Linux support, which provides a potentially useful foundation for SteamOS, but there is currently no confirmed official Steam Deck compatibility rating for this title. It should therefore not be described as Steam Deck Verified or officially Playable. Given its relatively simple visual-novel presentation and lightweight gameplay concept, experimentation on the handheld may be worthwhile, but players should be prepared for possible input, display, launcher, or runtime issues and should not assume flawless operation. The availability of a demo is particularly useful in this respect because it provides a practical way to test how the game behaves before committing to the complete experience.

Overall, Bermuda is an intriguing little experiment that benefits from knowing exactly what it wants to be. The alien-abduction scenario provides immediate tension, the questions surrounding trust give the story a psychological dimension, and the stealth puzzles add interaction to a format that can otherwise become mechanically passive. Full voice acting, configurable character voices, bonus conversations, original illustrations, and dedicated music further demonstrate considerable attention to presentation. Its short duration prevents the characters and setting from reaching their full potential, but it also produces a focused experience that can be completed without unnecessary filler. For players interested in unusual visual novels and compact science-fiction stories with a touch of stealth gameplay, it remains a distinctive if somewhat limited curiosity.

Rating: 6/10
